case_name: Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital c. E.L.
text:
Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital
c. E.L.

2023 QCCS 2094

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUÉBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

N°:

500-17-124694-236

DATE:

April 27, 2023

Reasons transcribed on May
30, 2023

______________________________________________________________________

IN THE PRESENCE OF:

THE HONOURABLE

CHRISTIAN J. BROSSARD, J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

SIR MORTIMER B. DAVIS JEWISH GENERAL HOSPITAL,
a
health institution administered by

the CIUSSS DU
CENTRE-OUEST-DE-L’ÎLE-DE-MONTRÉAL,

and

DR LOUISE MINER

Plaintiffs

v.

E. L.

Defendant-Concerned
Person

and

J.
S.

Interested
Person

and

CENTRE INTÉGRÉ UNIVERSITAIRE DE SANTÉ ET DE
SERVICES SOCIAUX DE L’OUEST-DE-L’îLE-DE-MONTRÉAL
(Douglas Mental Health University Institute)

Impleaded
party

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT RENDERED ORALLY
[1]

(Care)

______________________________________________________________________

A table of
content is included at the end of the judgment.

A.

INTRODUCTION
[2]

Ms. L.’s condition and situation

[
1
]

E. L., the person concerned by this proceeding,
is a 28-year-old woman who suffers from severe anorexia nervosa, more
specifically treatment refractory anorexia nervosa, with symptoms having begun
in early adolescence – one of the most severe cases seen by Dr. Robert
Biskin, her primary psychiatrist over the last year, under whose care Ms. L.
currently is at the Jewish General Hospital.

[
2
]

Despite extensive and expert treatments, – including
as authorized by successive judgments for the provision of care from the
Superior Court, the first one in December of 2019 –, Ms. L. spent
nearly all of the past five to six years in inpatient/residential treatment
programs or in hospitals, as a result of her condition, with the longest period
at home being five weeks in the fall of 2022, which followed a seven and a
half-month admission at the Jewish General Hospital.

[
3
]

Currently, Ms. L. has been hospitalized at
the Jewish General Hospital since November of 2022. While the last judgment for
the provision of care expired in December, she has been under confinement
orders from the Court of Québec, the latest one having been renewed until
mid-May of 2023.

[
4
]

Ms. L. also has several medical conditions
(listed at page 1 of Dr. Biskin’s report) that are consequences of her
severe anorexia nervosa, including a cardiac arrest in 2019, at age 24.

Treatment plan being sought

[
5
]

Presently, the Jewish General Hospital (the
Hospital
)
seeks a new order for the provision of care to Ms. L., pursuant to
article
16
of the
Civil Code of Québec
(CCQ), for both treatment and placement.

[
6
]

According to Dr. Biskin, who gave evidence as an
expert in psychiatry and whose report was filed as evidence, the required care,
and an order authorizing same, are necessary to avoid rapid deterioration of Ms. L.’s
physical condition and, put simply, death.

[
7
]

The treatment plan has three main components,
namely (1) treatment for Ms. L.’s physical condition (including
nutrition and hydration), (2) treatment for her psychiatric condition, which
treatments are more fully set out at pages 5 and 6 of Dr. Biskin's
report, and (3) a treatment setting.

[
8
]

The treatment setting would include a
residential resource “that can provide the needed care for as long as is
medically and psychiatrically necessary to ensure [Ms. L.’s] safety”. Depending
on her clinical evolution and as described at the time in Dr. Biskin's April 5,
2023 report, “this can include an acute care hospital (such as the Jewish
General Hospital), a specialized psychiatry institution (such as the Douglas
Mental Health Institute), a residential treatment program (affiliated or
recommended by the Douglas Mental Health Institute Eating Disorder Team), or a
CHSLD (or another long-term care unit that can provide and monitor her intake and
tube feedings), or other similar settings as necessary”. And, if Ms. L.’s
condition stabilizes while under the treatment order, a return at home could be
attempted if it is deemed safe by her treating team.
[3]

[
9
]

At the time of the hearing, three weeks after
Dr. Biskin’s report, the plan now was that Ms. L. be housed in a
CHSLD.

Ms. L.’s position

[
10
]

Ms. L. did not wish to be heard nor attend
the hearing. She did however retain counsel, with instructions to contest three
aspects of the treatment order being sought by the Hospital, namely:

1.

The housing in a CHSLD, her wish being to return
home with her mother, or, if that is not possible, to remain at the Jewish
General Hospital rather than go to a CHSLD;

2.

The five-year duration of the order being
sought, which should be limited to three years, especially in the context of
the housing; and

3.

The one-year maximum duration of anticipated rehospitalizations,
which should be a maximum of thirty days, which would provide enough time for
the Hospital to seek a longer duration.

[
11
]

As for the other elements required for an order
for care to be issued and the other elements of the treatment order being
sought, Ms. L. leaves them to this Court's determination.

B.

ANALYSIS

1.

Applicable law

[
12
]

In assessing the Hospital's application, this
Court must do so in accordance with the requirements of articles 12 and
16
CCQ,
and it must follow an analytical framework, apply criteria and abide by
guidelines established by the Court of Appeal.
[4]

2.

Capacity to consent

[
13
]

This Court has read Dr. Biskin's report and
heard his testimony.

[
14
]

Through his report and testimony, Dr. Biskin
explained how, even though Ms. L. has a theoretical understanding of
anorexia and recognizes that she has anorexia nervosa “by the label”, her
illness, which causes distortions in her perception of the reality of her
weight, her body and her physical condition, by its very nature affects her
judgment to a point where she is unable to understand the impact of her severe
anorexia nervosa on her health, and to a point where, while she clearly
indicates a desire to live and to have a meaningful life, she is unable to
understand that she will die without treatment or if she were without a
structure provided by a setting that can monitor her and ensure her stability.

[
15
]

And, even though Ms. L. understands that
feeding and gaining weight (or getting fat, as she sees it in her distorted
reality) will be helpful in addressing the acute risks to her health caused by,
or associated with, her condition, she is unable to act on that goal due to her
fear and lack of understanding of her situation.

[
16
]

In effect, because of her illness, Ms. L.
is unable to understand the extent of it, the consequences of such illness on
her health, the necessity of the treatment plan, and her lack of capacity to
independently follow through on the plan.

[
17
]

In short, Ms. L. is incapable of giving her
consent to the proposed treatment plan, including in terms of the setting for
the treatment of her physical and psychiatric conditions, which includes an
adapted place of housing.

3.

Categorical refusal

[
18
]

Ms. L. has a long-standing history of
treatment refusal and, even though she often agrees to treatment, there are
many unpredictable moments when she would suddenly refuse treatment and, more
importantly, she has a history of lying and of non-compliance with treatment,
both in and out of the hospital. This translates into and demonstrates a
categorical refusal of being treated.

[
19
]

Ms. L. has also categorically refused to be
placed in the safe and supervised setting that was proposed for and to her.

[
20
]

When out of a treatment setting, Ms. L.
does not follow the meal plan, and, at the hospital, she refuses food through
the mouth and throws food away. As a result, she receives most of her feeding
through a PEG feeding tube, but she has repeatedly said that she does not wish
to use the tube for feeding, to consume less calories. She has also refused to
have the time of the tube feeding changed to accommodate increased supervision
and improved oral intake. She has tried to refuse increases in the past as
well. When out of the hospital, she used the PEG tube unreliably. And there is
intermittent ongoing purging on her part.

[
21
]

During Ms. L.’s period of intense
dehydration, she tried to refuse IV fluid rehydration, to avoid what she
believed would cause weight gain, and only reluctantly, and only with the
authority of the court order for treatment in effect at the time, did she
receive IV fluid rehydration.

[
22
]

In other words, Ms. L. frequently refused,
and attempts to refuse, life-sustaining intervention required to keep her alive,
even though she wished, and she wishes, to continue to live. And, without the
court orders for the provision of care and the confinement order from the Court
of Québec currently in place, and without constant monitoring, Ms. L.
would be dead, according to Dr. Biskin.

[
23
]

Ms. L.’s categorical refusal of the
treatment required and being recommended for, and because of, her condition has
thus been demonstrated.

* *

[
24
]

In addition, while at home with her mother
during the fall of 2022, Ms. L. was ambivalent about attending an eating
disorder day program, leading to further reduced support, although she has
attended the Douglas Mental Health University Institute (the
Douglas Institute
)’s
Eating Disorder Unit inpatient treatment program (the
Douglas Eating
Disorder Program
or the
Program
) on numerous occasions in the past,
up until February of 2022, and for extended periods of time. Now, Ms. L.
sometimes does not want to attend a residential treatment program.

[
25
]

Ms. L. very clearly refuses to stay in a
long-term care setting such as a CHSLD.

[
26
]

In fact, Ms. L. will routinely request to
leave the hospital and return home with her mother, even when she is very
medically unstable. She repeatedly expresses different opinions about being in
a treatment setting, often requesting to leave the hospital (as already
mentioned, she is currently being kept against her will at the Jewish General
Hospital pursuant to the Court of Québec confinement order).

[
27
]

Again, Ms. L. categorical refusal has been
proven.

4.

Treatment plan

4.1.

Treatment of Ms. L.’s conditions

[
28
]

There is no doubt that, in terms of actual treatment,
including in terms of nutrition, hydration and addressing the severe medical
conditions resulting from Ms. L.’s malnutrition and dehydration, the
treatment being proposed, as explained by Dr. Biskin (more particularly,
at pages 5 and 6 of his report, sub-paragraphs 1 and 2), is in the best and
only interest of Ms. L., and that both its benefits and the risks of not
providing the treatment far outweigh the infringement on her fundamental rights
and any inconveniences from the treatment.

[
29
]

Without such treatment, death will ensue. To
quote Dr. Biskin, if medical treatment is not provided, Ms. L. “would be dead
and she has clearly and repeatedly expressed a desire to remain alive”.
[5]
In his report, Dr. Biskin also expanded
on the acute risks to Ms. L.’s health.
[6]

* *

[
30
]

That said, this judgment will require that
priority be given, as much as Ms. L.’s evolution and condition will allow
it, to the least intrusive, invasive and coercive means in terms of
administering the nutritional treatment.

[
31
]

This judgment will also require, in respect of
the requested possibility for the use of reasonable means of control, including
reasonable physical, mechanical and chemical restraints during the
administration of treatment, to prevent Ms. L. from interfering in the
treatment or in the case of agitation requiring sedation, that priority be
given, as much as possible, to the least coercive means (both physically and
chemically), with an obligation for the treating team to keep a detailed record
in Ms. L.’s medical file of any such restraints having been applied.

4.2.

Treatment setting

[
32
]

Also key to Ms. L.'s treatment is being
able to supervise and monitor her in a treatment setting.

[
33
]

Dr. Biskin made the point that Ms. L.
requires constant medical care and support to monitor medication compliance and
benefits, and for nutritional monitoring.

[
34
]

If Ms. L. were to leave a treatment center,
given her history of noncompliance with treatment, “she would either return or
die within weeks. Every attempt at discharge and recovery outside has been
foiled by her inability to gain or even maintain weight for more than a couple
of weeks in the community. As such, her functioning is extensively impaired by
her illness.”
[7]

[
35
]

Ms. L.’s physical condition when she was
readmitted to the hospital in November, five weeks after she had been
discharged, is evidence to that.

[
36
]

Consequently, even if Ms. L.’s mother (who
is terrified at the prospect of having her daughter come back home and, on the
contrary, supports the Hospital's application) were willing to take her
daughter back with her in the near future, this is not an option at present, nor
will it be one in the foreseeable future. According to Dr. Biskin,
Ms. L. would evidently return to the hospital in an underweight,
malnourished and dehydration state, or die within weeks.

[
37
]

Ms. L. therefore needs to be in a treatment
setting in a residential resource that can provide the care and the monitoring,
including the medical care and the medical monitoring that her particular
condition requires.

[
38
]

A CHSLD is such a treatment setting, as
explained by Dr. Biskin, including with the availability of physicians and the
possibility of sitters being available to monitor Ms. L.’s eating for
example, which would also ensure her medical stability and safety.

[
39
]

While the disadvantage of a CHSLD for Ms. L.
is that, on average, the residents on a medical floor are much older than she is,
unfortunately there are no other residential resources in Québec for people
with eating disorders.

[
40
]

That said, while such disadvantage and the fear
or apprehension it causes Ms. L. are not to be taken lightly, because of
the possible isolation or the loneliness that would quite likely ensue and
because of the anxiety it has caused her, and may continue to cause her, to
suffer (she has a diagnosis of anxiety disorder, for which she takes a number
of medications), the fact is that her loneliness is also her reality in the
hospital setting.

[
41
]

In fact, Ms. L. does not interact with
anyone at the hospital, other than her immediate caregivers. Instead, she is in
touch on a regular basis, using her phone or her tablet, with family, friends
or a network of people she has met through the Douglas Eating Disorder Program.

[
42
]

As for Ms. L. remaining as an inpatient at
the hospital indefinitely or for the longer term (as opposed to temporarily,
until the proper setting or CHSLD with availability has been identified), Dr. Biskin
explained why that is not a viable option. This can be summarised as follows:

1.

The Jewish General Hospital is an acute care
hospital, not a residential setting or a long-term care setting;

2.

Remaining in an acute care hospital is not the
longer-term treatment setting that Ms. L. requires, or that is best suited,
to treat her condition;

3.

As an acute care hospital, the Jewish General
Hospital has provided to Ms. L., over several years and over the last five
and a half months, a great deal of treatment without significant gains in terms
of her anorexia nervosa. In other words, while the Hospital has done everything
it could for Ms. L., given the lack of change over the past year,
remaining in an acute care setting such as a hospital is not beneficial to her;

4.

In that context, and without ignoring Ms. L.'s
best interest, and her best interest only, to the extent that a better-adapted
long-term treatment setting exists for her, namely a CHSLD, there is no
justifiable reason to take up one of the Hospital's limited beds that are
needed for other patients.

[
43
]

In other words, the CHSLD longer-term option
would provide the better support for Ms. L.'s condition, while ensuring a
better use of the Hospital's resources.

* *

[
44
]

As for the Douglas Institute’s Eating Disorder
Unit, which offers the Douglas Eating Disorder Program, an up to 12 to 16-week
inpatient program (the only such unit in Québec, with six beds available for
the province), it is not a viable option at this point.

[
45
]

Ms. L. attended the Program several times
in the past, including a six-month stay that ended in February of 2022. For her
to be admitted again, she would have to demonstrate some gains and stability.

[
46
]

In fact, since Dr. Biskin’s report, in which he
described the treatment settings envisioned at the time, one of the Douglas
Institute’s limited places in its Eating Disorder Unit became available for Ms. L..
Unfortunately, once informed of the possibility, she became anxious and
responded by restricting her food intake, which led to weight loss, and by
refusing treatment. This caused her to lose the spot.

[
47
]

As a result, and given Ms. L.’s previous
failed attempts going through the Program, and even though the possibility
remains – including if she is housed in a CHSLD – that she be able in the next
few months to reattend the Program, there are no assurances that this will be
so. She would first have to demonstrate enough motivation, with weight gains
and stability, to then be put on what is a long waiting list.

[
48
]

That said, being housed in a CHSLD would not
impair Ms. L.’s chances of being readmitted in the Program.

* *

[
49
]

Consequently, the situation is such that being
housed in a CHSLD is now, and for the foreseeable future, the only viable
option as a treatment setting for the appropriate housing and care of Ms. L.,
including in respect of her anorexia nervosa condition.

* *

[
50
]

Of course, a transfer to a CHSLD would not be
immediate. Following this judgment, Ms. L. will be put on a waiting list,
and the waiting time, before a place corresponding to her needs and her
situation is available, is unknown.

[
51
]

In the meantime, Ms. L. will continue to
receive the medical care and treatment for her condition at the Jewish General
Hospital, again without affecting either way the possibility of eventually
reintegrating the Douglas Eating Disorder Program.

* *

[
52
]

That said, once the Hospital has applied for a
place to be found for Ms. L. in a CHSLD, and has received a resulting
offer for such a place, and provided Ms. L.'s treating team is satisfied
that the proposed CHSLD is able to meet her particular needs, in terms of the
treatment she requires and the care required by her medical and psychiatric
conditions, and to ensure her safety, the Hospital will be required to apply
for the court's approval (possibly, but not necessarily, this Court) of the
selected CHSLD, with evidence at least from Dr. Biskin.

[
53
]

The Hospital will also be required to provide
information regarding:  (•) the
principal treating psychiatrist(s) or physician(s) who will have the leading
responsibility for following-up with the proper administration of the treatment
for Ms. L. once she has been transferred to the approved CHSLD, and (•) which of the Hospital or CHSLD (or
both) personnel will constitute the “treating team” as referenced in the
conclusions of this judgment.

[
54
]

The Hospital will necessarily have to proceed
quickly in obtaining the court's approval of the selected CHSLD. But this
judgment will provide for the possibility for the Hospital to accept the
proposed CHSLD, such acceptance to be conditional upon the court's approval, and
for an order that, once the Hospital has done so, the place be set aside for Ms. L.
for a period of 21 days, so that the Hospital may have time to apply for, and
obtain, the court's approval of the selected CHSLD without risking the loss of
the place during that period.

5.

Duration of the treatment order

[
55
]

Dr. Biskin explained why this matter is one of
the exceptional cases where the order should extend beyond three years, five
years in this instance.

[
56
]

Ms. L. has been sick for most of her life,
with her eating disorders starting when she was around 8 years old, and she has
continued to decline over the years. There have been two orders for the
provision of care for Ms. L., in connection with her anorexia nervosa
eating disorder, for durations of one year and two years respectively. There
have been multiple attempts at treatment over the past decade, including
several specialized treatment programs in the United States and in Canada,
without dramatic gain, and nothing seems to have changed. In fact, Ms. L.
has gotten worse in her eating disorder-type thoughts.

[
57
]

So, any treatment that will be necessary will be
a longer-term intervention.

[
58
]

The fact is that anorexia nervosa is different
than most psychiatric disorders where, as soon as you begin treatment with
medication, the medication usually helps within a foreseeable period. With
anorexia nervosa, the recovery duration is much longer, particularly the more
weight loss has occurred.

[
59
]

So, the treatment is extremely long, especially
given the intermittent refusal and sabotaging by Ms. L., by throwing her
food out, by purging, etc.

[
60
]

In short, with anorexia, treatment is longer. In
Ms. L.'s case, it has been particularly slow.

* *

[
61
]

Undoubtedly, that is all true. And the Court of
Appeal has stated that the duration of an order for care should both be “
la
plus courte qui est raisonnablement envisageable
sans neutraliser le
traitement
lui-même
” and a “
période suffisante pour s’assurer que le
traitement
produise les effets bénéfiques escomptés
”,
[8]
based on the circumstances of each case. Indeed, this can lead to
durations longer than one, two or even three years, including up to five years
as requested in this case.
[9]

[
62
]

However, because of the nature of Ms. L.’s
illness, the treatment she must submit to is quite an intrusive, invasive and
coercive one, including in terms of means of control to prevent her from
interfering in the treatment.

[
63
]

Plus, Ms. L. will be housed in a CHSLD, on
a medical floor or in a medical section where she will mostly be with people
much older than her.

[
64
]

All of that in the context of someone with
anxiety disorders.

[
65
]

Ms. L. should be allowed to preserve some
hope that, in a not-too-far-off future, she will see an end to her
“confinement” in a CHSLD.

[
66
]

In addition, it is this Court's view, based on
both Ms. L.'s young age and difficulties in submitting to treatment, and
on the intrusive, invasive and coercive nature of her required treatment, this
in a CHSLD setting, that her condition and her evolution through the treatment
should be submitted to judicial review in a not-too-distant future, relatively
speaking.

* *

[
67
]

The duration of the treatment order shall
therefore be set at 27 months.

[
68
]

A conclusion will, however, provide for the
possibility of a new application for the provision of care being presented without
awaiting the expiry of this judgment.

6.

Duration of anticipated rehospitalizations

[
69
]

This is a matter where there is a strong
possibility that, once Ms. L. has been discharged from the hospital, and
even if she is housed in a CHSLD, she may need to be readmitted in a hospital
for acute care.

[
70
]

Such possibility must be provided for,
particularly in the context of the very high risk of quick deterioration to Ms. L.’s
health and significant risk of death, if she fails to comply with her
treatment.

[
71
]

Again, with respect to duration, this is an
exceptional situation where, based on the nature of Ms. L.’s illness, and
considering the very long hospitalizations over the years – between six to nine
months each time –, it is clear that she does not respond and stabilize
quickly at all, and even the stability that she achieves falls quickly.

* *

[
72
]

That said, in keeping with the intent behind the
teachings of the Court of Appeal over the last two years,
[10]
and even though stabilizing Ms. L. will necessarily be a
matter of several months, a maximum allowance of sixty days should be provided
for at this moment, a period which should be enough to properly assess Ms. L.'s
condition to then apply to the court for a longer anticipated duration.

7.

Provisional execution

[
73
]

Dr. Biskin explained that, once Ms. L. is
aware that a judgment has been rendered, her typical response is to get very
anxious and to start restricting again, which would lead to more weight loss
and to a risk of significant physical consequences.

[
74
]

This is a case where, without an authorisation
for the immediate execution of this judgment, without having to wait for the
expiry of the five-day time limit for appealing,
[11]
the
situation presents a serious and imminent risk for the health of Ms. L., “
un
risque grave et imminent à [sa] santé
”, which establishes the justification
for an order of provisional execution.

[
75
]

Moreover, provisional execution will allow the Hospital
to immediately apply for a place for Ms. L. in a CHSLD, considering the
long delays inherent to the process.
[12]

FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT:

[1]

GRANTS
in part the
Originating Application to
Obtain Authorization from the Court for Care (Placement and Treatment)
(the

Application
) from Plaintiffs, Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General
Hospital, and Dr Louise Milner, in her capacity of director of
professional services of the Hospital (together, the
Hospital
);

[2]

AUTHORIZES
the Hospital to provide to the court, for
the purpose of the Application, the necessary documents and information contained
in the medical record of Defendant, E. L. (
Ms. L.
);

[3]

AUTHORIZES
the Hospital, and any institution,
physician or person designated by it, to administer the following treatment
plan to Ms. L., despite her categorical
refusal
,
respecting the guidelines given hereinafter:

a)

The administration and
monitoring

of nutritional supplements, nutrition,
fluids and hydration by any means, including by nasogastric tube, feeding tube,
percutaneous gastrostomy, G‑button feeding and/or intravenous, including
placement and replacement of said mean,

as deemed appropriate by Ms. L.’s
treating team based on her clinical evolution,

but
with priority given, as much as her evolution and condition allow it, to the
least intrusive, invasive and coercive means;

b)

The administration of
medication required to stabilize Ms. L.’s electrolytes, to protect her
kidney and her heart function, and of laxatives, as deemed appropriate by
Ms. L.’s treating team based on her clinical evolution and condition;

c)

The use of reasonable
means of control, including reasonable physical, mechanical and chemical
restraints, during the administration of treatment, to prevent Ms. L. from
interfering in the treatment or in the case of agitation requiring sedation,

but with priority given, as much as possible,
to the least coercive means (both physically and chemically),

with
an obligation for the treating team to keep a detailed record (dates and means
used) in Ms. L.’s medical file of any such restraints having been applied;

d)

The administration of
basic care and investigations to ensure safe treatment of Ms. L.’s
physical condition and of her psychiatric illness, such as blood tests for
therapeutic blood monitoring, vital signs monitoring, weight monitoring and
imaging if necessary, as deemed appropriate by Ms. L.’s treating team
based on her clinical evolution and condition;

[4]

AUTHORIZES
, as part of the treatment plan, the
Hospital, and any institution, physician or person designated by it, despite
Ms. L.’s categorical refusal, to transfer her to a CHSLD that can, in
addition to housing her, administer the treatment plan described in the
previous conclusion and that can provide the care required by her
medical and psychiatric conditions,
including treatment refractory anorexia nervosa, and to ensure her safety,
subject to the conclusions that follow;

[5]

ORDERS
that the CHSLD where Ms. L. is to be
transferred and housed in accordance with
the

previous conclusion be determined as follows:

a)

AUTHORIZES
the Hospital, and any physician or person
designated by it, to immediately apply for a place to be found for Ms. L.
in a CHSLD, with an objective of finding one that can meet her needs as
described in conclusion [4] above;

b)

AUTHORIZES
the Hospital, and any physician or person
designated by it, to accept a resulting offer for a place for Ms. L. in a
CHSLD, provided her treating team is satisfied that the proposed CHSLD is able
to meet her needs as described in conclusion [4] above (the
selected
CHSLD
);

c)

DECLARES
that the acceptance of the offer for a
place in the selected CHSLD by the Hospital shall be deemed conditional to the court
approving the selected CHSLD, as provided for in the following conclusions;

d)

ORDERS
that the accepted place in the selected
CHSLD be set aside for Ms. L. for a period of twenty-one (21) days
from such acceptance, so that the Hospital may apply for and obtain the court’s
approval of the selected CHSLD, as provided for in the following conclusions,
and inform the CHSLD of such approval before Ms. L. can be transferred to
the CHSLD;

e)

DECLARES
that the Hospital shall submit the
selected CHSLD for the court’s approval, so that the court may satisfy itself,
including with evidence from Dr Robert Biskin, that the selected CHSLD is
able to meet Ms. L.’s needs as described in conclusion [4] above;

f)

DECLARES
that the Hospital shall also, as part of
its application pursuant to the previous conclusion, (i) identify for the court,
to its satisfaction, the treating psychiatrist(s) or physician(s) who will have
the leading responsibility for following-up on the proper administration of the
treatment to Ms. L. once she has been transferred to the approved CHSLD
and (ii) which of the Hospital or CHSLD (or both)’s personnel will
constitute the “treating team” as referenced in the conclusions of this
judgment;

g)

DECLARES
that it shall be the Hospital’s
responsibility to ensure, through its lawyers, that the application for the court’s
approval of the selected CHSLD is filed promptly and timely, with enough prior
notice so as to be set down for hearing soon enough to be able to inform the
CHSLD of such approval within the 21-day delay provided for in the conclusion
at subparagraph d) above, or to obtain an extension of the delay;

[6]

ORDERS
that Ms. L. not be transferred to a
CHSLD until the approval of the selected CHSLD (the
approved CHSLD
) has
been given by the court in accordance with the previous conclusion;

[7]

AUTHORIZES
the CIUSSS de l’Ouest-de-l’Île-de-Montréal
and the administrator of the approved CHSLD to house Ms. L. at the
approved CHSLD, despite her
categorical
refusal and against her will;

[8]

DECLARES
that, once Ms. L. has been
transferred to the approved CHSLD, the latter shall administer the treatment
plan authorized for her in accordance with this judgment;

[9]

DECLARES
that, notwithstanding conclusion [7]
above, Ms. L. shall not be prevented from attending the
Douglas Mental Health Institute Eating
Disorder Unit’s inpatient treatment program or other similar programs as
deemed appropriate by her treating team
and if a place is available for her;

[10]

AUTHORIZES
the Hospital to pursue the hospitalization
of Ms. L. until her condition is stabilized and until a safe discharge
plan is in place;

[11]

ORDERS
Ms. L., as part of the treatment
plan, to attend regular follow-up appointments, if required outside of the
hospital or of the CHSLD settings, as the case may be, as deemed appropriate by
her treating team, with an outpatient psychiatry team or clinic, such as the
Douglas Mental Health University Institute eating disorder team, or any other
follow-up as deemed appropriate by Ms. L.’s treating team, in order to
provide her with the support that she needs, to receive her treatment, and to
allow her treating team to monitor her medical, psychiatric and psychosocial
condition, including nutritional monitoring, and her clinical evolution;

[12]

ORDERS
that if Ms. L.’s condition
deteriorates or if she fails to comply with the treatment plan, she be
transported to the Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital (if the main
risk is of physical deterioration) or to the

Douglas
Mental Health University Institute (if the main risk is of psychiatric
deterioration) or to any other hospital setting, by ambulance or a peace
officer, upon request of any member of her treating team, and that she be
hospitalized so that her medical, psychiatric and psychosocial conditions may
be assessed and stabilized and that treatment be resumed and/or adjusted, until
her condition is stable enough to allow for discharge, for a duration however
that may not exceed sixty (60) days without having obtained an order from the court
authorizing a longer hospitalization;

[13]

ORDERS
any peace officer to use the necessary
means, including the necessary force, to assist the Hospital, or any
institution or physician or person designated by it, in the execution of the
judgment, if Ms. L. refuses to comply with the judgment;

[14]

ORDERS
any treating physician of Ms. L. to,
every six (6) months, report to the Counsel of Physicians, Dentists and
Pharmacists ("CPDP") of the CIUSSS du
Centre-Ouest-de-l’Île-de-Montréal or to the CPDP of any other institution
designated by the Hospital, on the evolution of Ms. L.’s health and her
general condition;

[15]

ORDERS
that, in case of diverging opinions between
Ms. L.’s treating physician and the CPDP, the difference of opinion be
submitted to the court;

[16]

ORDERS
that the conclusions of this judgment be
applicable, with the necessary adjustments, by any health institution, treating
team or treating doctor in charge of Ms. L., and
AUTHORIZES
the
Hospital and any health institution, treating team and treating doctor in
charge of Ms. L. to exchange information about her in order to ensure
adequate follow-up, monitoring and
the proper execution of this judgment;

[17]

DECLARES
that this judgment shall be valid for a
duration of twenty-seven (27 months);

[18]

ALLOWS
the Hospital and the
CIUSSS du
Centre-Ouest-de-l’Île-de-Montréal, if, no more than three (3) months prior to
the expiry of this judgment, it has determined that it will ask for the renewal
of this judgment or for a new order for the provision of care to Ms. L.,
to present its application without waiting for the expiry of this judgment;

[19]

ORDERS
the provisional execution of this judgment
notwithstanding appeal;

[20]

THE WHOLE
without legal costs.
